questions.question: What is GitHub Flow and how does it differ from GitFlow?
questions.title: GitHub Flow vs GitFlow
questions.direct_answer: **GitHub Flow** keeps one default branch and uses short-lived topic branches proposed through pull requests; accepted changes are deployed according to the project's release process. **GitFlow** adds long-lived development and temporary release/hotfix branches for a more staged release model. CI, required reviews, feature flags, and automatic deployment are useful policies but not definitions guaranteed by either workflow.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that GitHub Flow is a deliberate continuous-delivery model, not just GitFlow with branches removed, and can name the trade-offs (CI strength, feature flags) that make it work
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating GitHub Flow as 'GitFlow-lite' and keeping feature branches alive for weeks, which reintroduces the merge pain the model is designed to avoid
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that GitHub Flow pushes the safety net onto automated tests and feature flags, and that the choice between the two workflows is driven by release cadence — continuous deploy vs scheduled releases

sections.title: GitHub Flow: Simplicity Built for Continuous Delivery
sections.content:
**GitHub Flow** is a minimalist branching strategy for teams that deploy continuously — often many times per day. It has only two kinds of branches: **main** (always production-ready) and **short-lived feature branches** (usually one to three days).

The whole loop is: branch off `main`, commit, open a **pull request**, let CI run, get a review, merge, and deploy. There is no `develop` integration branch, no `release` branch, and no `hotfix` branch. The single rule that makes this safe is that **`main` is always shippable** — every merged commit is tested and ready for production. A bug fix is just another short-lived branch.

**GitFlow**, by contrast, is a five-branch model (`main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`) built for *scheduled* releases. GitHub Flow removes release-branch ceremony. Teams commonly add automated tests and may use feature flags when they need to merge code before releasing behavior.

sections.title: GitHub Flow at a Glance
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[main
always deployable] --> B[create
feature branch] B --> C[commit +
push] C --> D[open Pull Request
CI runs tests] D --> E[review +
address feedback] E --> F[merge to main] F --> G[auto-deploy
to production] G --> A ```

sections.title: GitHub Flow vs GitFlow
sections.content:
| Aspect | GitHub Flow | GitFlow |
|---|---|---|
| **Branches** | `main` + feature branches | `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*` |
| **Release model** | Continuous deployment | Scheduled / versioned releases |
| **Branch lifetime** | Hours to a few days | Days to weeks |
| **Where features start** | From `main` | From `develop` |
| **Hotfixes** | A normal short branch off `main` | Dedicated `hotfix/*`, merged to `main` AND `develop` |
| **Best for** | SaaS, web apps, microservices | Enterprise apps with QA gates, multiple supported versions |
| **Depends on** | Strong CI + feature flags | Release discipline + a release manager |

sections.title: Anti-pattern: a long-lived feature branch (GitFlow habits in GitHub Flow)
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher branches once and disappears for two weeks
git checkout -b feature/big-checkout-rewrite
# ...30 commits, no PR, no integration...

# Two weeks later main has moved on a lot
git checkout main
git merge feature/big-checkout-rewrite
# CONFLICT in 11 files — a painful 'big bang' merge
# This defeats the entire point of GitHub Flow
```

sections.title: GitHub Flow done right: small, short-lived branch + PR
sections.content:
```bash
# Start from an up-to-date main
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b fix-null-order-lookup

# Small change in OrderService.java, commit and push
git add src/main/java/com/example/service/OrderService.java
git commit -m "fix: handle missing order in OrderService"
git push origin fix-null-order-lookup

# Open a PR on GitHub -> CI runs JUnit tests automatically
# After approval, merge -> CD deploys to production
git checkout main && git pull origin main
git branch -d fix-null-order-lookup
```
*Branch lives hours, not weeks — conflicts stay tiny and feedback is fast.*

sections.title: When to Pick Each Workflow
sections.content:
**Reach for GitHub Flow when** your Java service deploys continuously (SaaS, microservices), production is a single environment, your team is small to medium, and you have a strong CI pipeline running tests on every PR. Use feature flags when you intentionally need deployment and user release to happen at different times.

**Reach for GitFlow when** you ship on a schedule, need formal QA/staging approval gates (banking, regulated systems), or must maintain several production versions at once (supporting v1.x while building v2.x).

Don't use GitHub Flow without solid automated tests — you're trusting CI instead of a manual QA phase. Don't use GitFlow for high-velocity web apps where its ceremony just slows you down.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating it as GitFlow-lite**: the simplicity is the point — it optimizes for fast feedback, not scheduled releases.
- **Long-lived feature branches**: branches that live for weeks recreate the merge pain GitHub Flow avoids. Slice work into small PRs or hide it behind a flag.
- **Weak or missing CI**: merging straight to `main` with no automated tests is shipping without brakes — GitHub Flow leans entirely on CI to catch regressions.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- GitHub Flow uses a default branch plus short-lived topic branches and pull requests.
- GitFlow adds `develop` and defined feature, release, and hotfix branch roles.
- GitHub Flow suits simpler, frequent integration; GitFlow models staged/versioned releases.
- CI, review requirements, deployment, and feature flags are repository practices—not automatic GitHub Flow features.
- Choose based on release cadence, support branches, compliance, and team cost.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: GitHub Flow is a lightweight workflow built around one rule: the main branch is always deployable. When I need to add a feature or fix a bug, I branch off main, make small commits, and push the branch. Then I open a pull request so my team can review it, and while it's open our CI pipeline runs all the tests and builds the app. Teammates leave comments, I address them with more commits, and once everyone approves and CI is green, I merge into main. At that point our deployment pipeline ships the code to production automatically, usually within minutes, and then I delete the branch. The whole thing takes hours or a day, not weeks. The big difference from GitFlow is simplicity: there's no develop branch, no release branches, and no hotfix branches. Every change follows the same path — branch, pull request, review, merge, deploy. That works really well for web apps and microservices that deploy continuously. The trade-off is less release-branch structure, so the team needs an explicit testing and deployment policy. Feature flags are one optional way to release behavior later. So if I'm building something big, I'd merge small pieces daily behind a flag, and flip the flag on once it's ready. GitFlow makes more sense when you ship on a schedule, need formal QA gates, or support several versions at once.

followup_questions: What is trunk-based development and how does it compare to GitHub Flow?
How do feature flags let you merge incomplete features to main safely?
Why does GitHub Flow depend so heavily on continuous integration?

questions.question: What is a .gitignore file and what should go in it?
questions.title: .gitignore Basics
questions.direct_answer: A **`.gitignore`** file contains patterns for intentionally untracked files that Git should normally leave untracked. Typical entries include reproducible build output, editor-specific files, logs, caches, and machine-local configuration. It does not affect files already tracked and is not a security control: exposed credentials must be rotated and may need removal from history.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows what should never be committed and understands that .gitignore does not retroactively untrack files already in history
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding target/ or a secrets file to .gitignore after it was already committed and assuming it's now ignored — Git keeps tracking it because it was committed first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that secrets in history stay forever even after deletion, so the real fix is rotating the credential, and mention gitignore.io to generate stack-specific templates

sections.title: The .gitignore File: Keeping the Repository Clean
sections.content:
A **`.gitignore`** file is a plain text file (usually in the repo root) that tells Git which files and directories to ignore — Git won't stage, track, or commit anything matching its patterns.

The goal is **repository hygiene**: only source code and shared configuration belong in version control. Generated **build output** like Maven's `target/` (compiled `.class` files, packaged JARs) is reproducible from source, so committing it just bloats the repo and causes conflicts. **IDE files** like IntelliJ's `.idea/` shouldn't be shared because teammates may use a different editor. And **secrets** — database passwords, API keys — must never enter Git history.

Pattern syntax is simple: `target/` ignores a directory, `*.log` ignores all log files, and a leading `!` makes an exception (`!keep.log`). A `.gitignore` only governs *untracked* files — if something was committed before you ignored it, Git keeps tracking it until you explicitly untrack it.

sections.title: What Belongs in .gitignore at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build output|~Generated from source|target/|build/, .gradle/|*.class
blue|IDE files|~Per-developer, not shared|.idea/|*.iml|.vscode/
emerald|Logs & OS junk|~Usually local noise|*.log, logs/|.DS_Store|Thumbs.db
rose|Local secrets|~Not a security boundary|.env|application-local.properties|API keys

sections.title: Step 1 — Create the .gitignore Before Your First Commit
sections.content:
Create the file at the repository root so its rules apply to the whole project recursively. The most reliable starting point is a generated template from [gitignore.io](https://www.toptal.com/developers/gitignore) for `Java, Maven, Gradle, IntelliJ` — it covers edge cases you'd otherwise miss.

| Pattern | What it ignores |
|---|---|
| `target/` | Maven build output |
| `build/`, `.gradle/` | Gradle build output |
| `*.class` | compiled bytecode |
| `.idea/`, `*.iml` | IntelliJ project files |
| `*.log`, `logs/` | log files |
| `.env`, `application-local.properties` | local secrets |
| `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db` | OS junk |

sections.title: Step 2 — A Realistic Java .gitignore
sections.content:
```bash
# Maven build output
target/

# Gradle build output
build/
.gradle/

# Compiled class files
*.class

# IDE files
.idea/
*.iml
.vscode/

# Logs
*.log
logs/

# Local config with secrets (NEVER commit these)
application-local.properties
application-local.yml
.env

# OS junk
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Exception: keep the shared default config
!src/main/resources/application.properties
```

sections.title: The classic trap: ignoring a file that's already committed
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher commits everything first, including target/
git add .
git commit -m "initial commit"   # target/ is now tracked

# Later they add target/ to .gitignore...
echo "target/" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore && git commit -m "add gitignore"

# ...but target/ STILL shows up in every commit
git status   # target/ files still tracked! .gitignore is ignored for them
```

sections.title: The fix: untrack with git rm --cached, then ignore
sections.content:
```bash
# Stop tracking target/ but KEEP it on disk
git rm -r --cached target/

# Now .gitignore takes over
echo "target/" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: stop tracking build output"

# git status is finally clean of target/
```
*For a leaked secret, untracking isn't enough — it stays in history, so you must rotate the credential immediately.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Committing build output**: tracking `target/` bloats the repo and causes spurious conflicts on every build.
- **Adding to .gitignore too late**: a file committed before being ignored stays tracked — you need `git rm --cached`.
- **Leaking secrets**: committing `application-local.properties` with a DB password is a security incident; deleting the file later doesn't help because it's in history forever — rotate the credential.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `.gitignore` patterns apply to intentionally untracked paths.
- Common entries include build output, caches, logs, editor files, and machine-local configuration.
- Do not ignore source, build definitions, or shared configuration just because it is inconvenient.
- Already tracked files are unaffected; `git rm --cached` can stop future tracking.
- Ignoring a secret does not erase history or revoke it—rotate exposed credentials.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A gitignore file tells Git which files to never track or commit. It usually sits in the project root and contains patterns for things you want to exclude. For a Java project I'd ignore the build output, like Maven's target folder, because that's full of compiled class files and packaged JARs that are generated from source, so there's no point versioning them. I'd also ignore IDE files like IntelliJ's dot-idea folder, because teammates might use a different editor. Machine-local secret files are normally ignored, but `.gitignore` is only a guard against accidental addition. Secret scanning and credential rotation are still required. Those belong in environment variables or a secrets manager. I'd also ignore log files and OS junk like dot-DS-Store on Mac. The syntax is simple: a name with a trailing slash ignores a directory, star-dot-log ignores all log files, and a leading exclamation mark makes an exception. The classic mistake freshers make is committing the target folder first, then adding it to gitignore later and being surprised it's still tracked. Gitignore only affects untracked files, so for something already committed you have to run git rm minus r minus minus cached to untrack it. And the worst mistake is committing a secret, because even if you delete the file, it stays in history forever, so the real fix is rotating that credential. When I start a project I generate a template from gitignore dot io for Java, Maven, and my IDE so I don't miss anything.

followup_questions: How do you untrack a file that was accidentally committed?
Why isn't deleting a leaked secret file enough, and what should you do instead?
What is a global gitignore and when would you use one?

questions.question: What are conventional commits and why do teams use them?
questions.title: Conventional Commits
questions.direct_answer: **Conventional Commits** defines a parseable header such as `feat(parser): add CSV support`, with optional body and footers. The specification gives special meaning to `feat`, `fix`, and breaking changes; teams may define other types. Changelog generation or version bumps happen only when release tooling is configured to use the messages.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the commit type drives automation (versioning, changelogs) rather than being a cosmetic style rule
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using the wrong type — writing feat for a bug fix or forgetting to flag a breaking change — which produces an incorrect automated version bump
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how BREAKING CHANGE or the ! suffix triggers a major version bump, and that commitlint git hooks enforce the format so malformed messages are rejected

sections.title: Conventional Commits: Machine-Readable Commit Messages
sections.content:
**Conventional Commits** is a lightweight specification for writing commit messages that both humans and tools can parse. The format is **`type(scope): description`** — for example `feat(auth): add JWT refresh endpoint`.

The **type** is a category: `feat` (new feature), `fix` (bug fix), `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore` (maintenance), and a few others. The **scope** in parentheses is optional and names the affected area.

Why bother? Because the structured prefix unlocks **automation**. Tools like `semantic-release` read the types to compute the next version: a `fix` bumps the patch, a `feat` bumps the minor, and a breaking change bumps the major. Changelog generators group commits into *Features* and *Bug Fixes* sections automatically, and you can search history with `git log --grep '^feat'`. Without the tooling it's just convention; with it, your release pipeline runs itself.

sections.title: Commit Types at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|feat|~New feature|minor version bump|user-facing capability|shows up in changelog
amber|fix|~Bug fix|patch version bump|corrects behavior|shows up in changelog
blue|docs / refactor / test|~No release impact|no version bump|internal or cosmetic|kept out of changelog
rose|BREAKING CHANGE / feat!|~Incompatible change|major version bump|breaks clients|must be flagged explicitly

sections.title: Step 1 — Learn the Type → Version-Bump Mapping
sections.content:
Pick the type that matches what the commit actually does, because it directly controls the released version under **semantic versioning** (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`).

| Type | Meaning | SemVer effect |
|---|---|---|
| `fix:` | bug fix | patch (1.2.0 → 1.2.1) |
| `feat:` | new feature | minor (1.2.0 → 1.3.0) |
| `feat!:` / `BREAKING CHANGE:` | backward-incompatible change | major (1.2.0 → 2.0.0) |
| `docs:` | documentation only | none |
| `refactor:` | restructure, no behavior change | none |
| `test:` / `chore:` | tests / tooling | none |

sections.title: Step 2 — Write Real Conventional Commits
sections.content:
```bash
# Feature with a scope -> minor bump
git commit -m "feat(order): add order cancellation endpoint"

# Bug fix with a body explaining the why
git commit -m "fix(payment): prevent duplicate charge on double-click" \
           -m "Added a Redis idempotency key to deduplicate requests."

# Breaking change -> major bump (note the !)
git commit -m "feat(auth)!: shorten token expiry from 24h to 1h" \
           -m "BREAKING CHANGE: clients must implement token refresh."

# Maintenance and docs -> no version bump
git commit -m "chore(deps): upgrade Spring Boot 3.1.0 -> 3.2.0"
git commit -m "docs(readme): add local PostgreSQL setup steps"
```

sections.title: Vague messages that break automation
sections.content:
```bash
# No type prefix -> tooling can't categorize or version it
git commit -m "added feature"

# Wrong type -> versioning bumps the wrong number
git commit -m "feat: fix typo in error message"   # really a fix!

# Breaking change not flagged -> major version never bumps
git commit -m "feat: change API response shape"   # silently breaks clients
```

sections.title: Correct types let release tooling do the work
sections.content:
```bash
# Right type, clear scope
git commit -m "fix(i18n): correct typo in validation message"

# Breaking change explicitly flagged
git commit -m "feat(api)!: change response shape to envelope format" \
           -m "BREAKING CHANGE: 'data' is now nested under a root object."
```
*With these, semantic-release picks the right version and the changelog writes itself; commitlint as a git hook rejects malformed messages before they land.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating it as a style guide**: the value is automation — without tools reading the types, it's just ceremony.
- **Wrong type**: labeling a fix as `feat` bumps the minor version instead of the patch, producing a misleading release.
- **Unflagged breaking changes**: changing a public API without `BREAKING CHANGE:`/`!` leaves the major version stuck and breaks clients who upgrade expecting compatibility.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Format: `<type>[optional scope][!]: <description>` with optional body and footers.
- `feat` marks a feature and `fix` marks a bug fix.
- A `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer marks an incompatible change.
- Other types such as `docs`, `test`, or `chore` are allowed but team-defined.
- Automation is a benefit only when configured release tools consume the convention.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Conventional Commits is a specification for writing commit messages in a structured format that both people and tools can read. The format is a type, an optional scope in parentheses, a colon, and then a description. The type is a category like feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, docs for documentation, refactor for restructuring without behavior change, or chore for maintenance. So a message might be feat, scope auth, colon, add JWT refresh endpoint. The reason teams use it is automation. A tool like semantic-release reads the types and figures out the next version: if there are only fixes, it bumps the patch; if there's a feature, it bumps the minor; and if there's a breaking change, it bumps the major. You signal a breaking change with an exclamation mark after the type, or a BREAKING CHANGE line in the body. It also generates changelogs automatically by grouping commits into features and bug fixes, and it makes history searchable. The mistake freshers make is thinking it's just a style guide to look professional — the real value only shows up when tools parse it. The other mistake is using the wrong type, like writing feat when you actually fixed a bug, because that bumps the wrong version number. And you have to flag breaking changes explicitly, otherwise the major version won't bump and you'll break clients who expected backward compatibility. Teams usually enforce all this with a tool called commitlint that runs as a git hook and rejects messages that don't follow the format.

followup_questions: How does semantic versioning map to fix, feat, and breaking changes?
How would you enforce conventional commits across a team?

questions.question: What is GitFlow and what are its main branches?
questions.title: GitFlow Workflow Explained
questions.direct_answer: **GitFlow** is a release-oriented branching model with long-lived `main` (originally `master`) and `develop` branches plus temporary `feature/*`, `release/*`, and `hotfix/*` branches. In the classic model, releases and hotfixes are integrated back into both production and development lines. Teams often adapt these rules, and simpler workflows may fit continuous delivery better.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the five branch types, where features originate (develop, not main), and the merge rules — especially that hotfixes go back to both main and develop
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Branching features from main instead of develop, or merging a hotfix only into main and letting develop reintroduce the bug at the next release
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that GitFlow is heavyweight for continuous deployment and many modern teams prefer GitHub Flow or trunk-based development for high-velocity delivery

sections.title: GitFlow: Structured Branching for Scheduled Releases
sections.content:
**GitFlow** is a branching model (created by Vincent Driessen) designed for projects with **scheduled releases** — common in enterprise Java applications with dev, staging, and production environments.

It has two permanent branches and three supporting ones: **`main`** holds production-ready code where release commits are tagged; **`develop`** is the integration branch where finished features come together. **`feature/*`** branches start from `develop` and merge back into it. **`release/*`** branches fork from `develop` to stabilize a version (only bug fixes, no new features), then merge into both `main` and `develop`. **`hotfix/*`** branches fork from `main` to patch a live bug fast, then merge into both `main` and `develop`.

The strict rules prevent chaos but require discipline — you can't just commit to `main` whenever you like. That structure is exactly why GitFlow feels heavyweight for teams that deploy many times a day.

sections.title: GitFlow Branches and Merges
sections.content:
```mermaid
gitGraph
  commit id: "v1.0" tag: "v1.0"
  branch develop
  checkout develop
  commit
  branch feature/login
  checkout feature/login
  commit
  commit
  checkout develop
  merge feature/login
  branch release/1.1
  checkout release/1.1
  commit id: "bump 1.1"
  checkout main
  merge release/1.1 tag: "v1.1"
  checkout develop
  merge release/1.1
```

sections.title: The Five Branches and Their Merge Rules
sections.content:
Walk the lifecycle the way it actually runs in a team:

- **`main`** — always production-ready; release commits are tagged (for example `v1.2.0`). Nobody commits here directly.
- **`develop`** — the integration branch; the latest delivered-but-unreleased work lives here.
- **`feature/*`** — branch from `develop`, build one feature, merge back to `develop` (often with `--no-ff` to preserve grouping).
- **`release/*`** — branch from `develop` when a version is feature-complete; only bug fixes and version bumps allowed; merge into **both** `main` (tag it) **and** `develop`.
- **`hotfix/*`** — branch from `main` for an urgent production bug; merge into **both** `main` (new patch tag) **and** `develop` so the fix isn't lost.

The two 'merge into both' rules are the interview trap — releases and hotfixes always flow back to `develop`.

sections.title: Mistake: branching a feature from main and losing a hotfix
sections.content:
```bash
# Wrong: feature started from main, not develop
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/user-auth   # diverges from production line

# Wrong: hotfix merged ONLY into main
git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix/npe-on-login
git commit -m "fix: guard against null user"
git checkout main && git merge hotfix/npe-on-login
# forgot develop -> next release reintroduces the same bug
```

sections.title: Correct GitFlow: features from develop, hotfix into both
sections.content:
```bash
# Feature branches off develop and merges back to develop
git checkout develop && git pull
git checkout -b feature/user-auth
git commit -m "feat: add JWT validation"
git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff feature/user-auth

# Hotfix off main, merged into BOTH main and develop
git checkout main && git checkout -b hotfix/npe-on-login
git commit -m "fix: guard against null user"
git checkout main && git merge --no-ff hotfix/npe-on-login
git tag -a v1.2.1 -m "hotfix release"
git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff hotfix/npe-on-login
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Branching features from `main`**: features must start from `develop`, the integration branch.
- **Hotfix only into `main`**: forgetting to merge it back into `develop` means the bug returns at the next release.
- **Using GitFlow for continuous deployment**: the model assumes infrequent, tested releases — it feels bureaucratic when you ship five times a day.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Five branches** — `main`, `develop`, `feature/*`, `release/*`, `hotfix/*`.
- **Features start from `develop`**, never from `main`.
- **`release/*` and `hotfix/*` merge into BOTH `main` and `develop`.**
- **Releases on `main` are tagged** in the classic model.
- **Heavyweight by design** — great for scheduled releases, overkill for continuous deploy.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: GitFlow is a branching model with five branch types that control how code moves from development to production. The two permanent branches are main, which represents the production release line, and develop, where all features integrate. When I start a new feature, like user authentication, I branch off develop, not main — that's a detail freshers often get wrong. I do my work, commit, and merge back into develop, usually with the no-fast-forward flag so the history stays grouped. Once develop has enough for a release, we cut a release branch from it, do final testing and bug fixes only — no new features — and then merge that into both main and develop, tagging main with the version number. If a serious bug hits production, we create a hotfix branch off main, fix it, and merge it back into both main and develop. That last part is the key thing interviewers look for: hotfixes and releases always go back to develop too, because if you only merge a hotfix into main, the next release built from develop will reintroduce the same bug. GitFlow works really well for enterprise projects with scheduled releases every few weeks and formal QA stages, but it's overkill if you're deploying continuously. Many modern teams use simpler models like GitHub Flow or trunk-based development because GitFlow's ceremony slows down fast iteration.

questions.question: What is trunk-based development?
questions.title: Trunk-Based Development
questions.direct_answer: **Trunk-based development** integrates small changes into one shared trunk frequently. Developers either commit directly under strong controls or use very short-lived branches. Feature flags can separate deployment from release, but they are optional; branch by abstraction and incremental delivery are other ways to keep unfinished changes safe.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows trunk-based development still uses (short-lived) branches and depends on feature flags and strong CI rather than being chaotic 'commit to main' free-for-all
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing trunk-based development means no branches at all, or attempting it without feature flags and comprehensive automated tests
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that frequent integration shrinks merge conflicts and that feature flags decouple deploy from release, letting incomplete code ship hidden behind a toggle

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- One shared trunk is the main integration line.
- Changes are small and integrated frequently; any branches are short-lived.
- Fast automated feedback and disciplined review reduce the risk of frequent integration.
- Feature flags are optional tools for separating deployment from release.
- The goal is low divergence and continuous integration, not unreviewed commits or half-built behavior in production.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Trunk-based development is a workflow where everyone integrates small changes into one shared branch, the trunk, several times a day. Branches do exist, but they're extremely short-lived — usually a few hours, two days at most. The idea is to integrate constantly so conflicts and bugs show up early, instead of working alone for weeks and then hitting a giant merge. Companies like Google use this because it lets them deploy hundreds of times a day. Feature flags are one common tool when deployed code must remain unavailable to users. Say I'm building a new checkout flow. I'd merge the first piece to the trunk the same day, but wrap it in a feature flag so it's hidden in production. The next day I add the payment step and merge again, still behind the flag. So the feature is sitting in production the whole time, just dark, and when it's done I flip the flag to release it. That separates deploying the code from releasing the feature. The mistake freshers make is thinking trunk-based means no branches or that it's chaotic — you still use short-lived branches and pull requests. The other mistake is integrating changes without any safe incremental-delivery technique, which can expose incomplete behavior. And you absolutely need strong automated tests and fast CI, because if you're merging ten times a day, the tests are what keep production stable. The payoff is far fewer merge conflicts and really fast feedback, but it takes discipline: small commits, high coverage, and a mature pipeline.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Trunk-based development keeps one shared branch as the main integration line and limits how far work can diverge from it. Small changes are integrated frequently, either directly under suitable controls or through short-lived branches.

The method does not require every developer to push several times per day, nor does it require feature flags for every change. A team can use incremental slices, branch by abstraction, backward-compatible database changes, or a feature flag when deployment must happen before user release.

The supporting practices are fast feedback, reliable tests, small reviews, and a way to stop incomplete behavior from affecting users. The boundary is important: a long-lived integration branch called `develop` is no longer serving as the trunk, while an unreviewed free-for-all on `main` is not a mature trunk-based workflow.

sections.title: Deploy vs Release with Feature Flags
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[small change
short-lived branch] --> B[PR + CI
under 10 min] B --> C[merge to trunk
several times/day] C --> D[deploy to prod
flag OFF] D --> E[finish feature
over a few days] E --> F[flip flag ON
= release] ```

sections.title: Feature Flag + Frequent Integration in Practice
Anti-pattern: long-lived branch, no flag
sections.content:
```bash
# Three-week branch with no integration and no flag
git checkout -b feature/checkout-rewrite
# ...many commits, main drifts far ahead...
git checkout main && git merge feature/checkout-rewrite
# Huge conflict, and half-built checkout is now visible in prod
```

sections.title: Trunk-based: tiny increments behind a flag
sections.content:
```bash
# Day 1: skeleton behind flag, merged same day
git checkout -b add-checkout-skeleton
git commit -am "feat: checkout skeleton behind FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT"
git checkout main && git merge add-checkout-skeleton && git push

# Day 2: payment step, still flagged off
git commit -am "feat: payment validation in new checkout"
git push origin main
# Feature is in prod the whole time, just hidden until the flag flips
```
*Conflicts stay small because the trunk never drifts far from your work.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking it means no branches**: branches exist, they're just very short-lived and merged via PR.
- **No safe release technique**: use flags, backward-compatible slices, or another deliberate method when work cannot be released yet.
- **Weak tests / slow CI**: merging to trunk ten times a day needs high coverage and CI under ten minutes, or you'll break production constantly.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: **GitHub Flow** is a lightweight, two-branch workflow: `main` is always deployable, and every change lives on a short-lived **feature branch** merged back through a **pull request** after CI and review. Unlike **GitFlow**, it has no `develop`, `release`, or `hotfix` branches — that simplicity is deliberate and relies on strong CI plus **feature flags** to hide unfinished work in production.
